title: The Original Queen Made Kangana a Star. Now Its Sequel Is Being Sued for ₹250 Crore.
excerpt: Phantom Studios claims Queen 2 is an unauthorised sequel and has taken the fight to the Bombay High Court — just as the film finishes shooting.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Phantom Studios is suing JioStar for ₹250 crore over Queen 2's unauthorized sequel.
  • Phantom claims 50% ownership of Queen's intellectual property rights.
  • The lawsuit follows Queen 2's completion of principal photography.
  • Phantom Films, now dissolved, produced iconic films including Queen and Gangs of Wasseypur.
  • The case could set a precedent for sequel rights in Indian cinema.

Phantom Studios lawsuit details
https://youtube.com/watch?v=Smwz58YACT4 The original **Queen** was a miracle. A film nobody believed in — not the studio, not the market, not even its own production company — that became one of the defining Bollywood films of the 2010s. It made **Kangana Ranaut** into a superstar. It made **Vikas Bahl** into a name. And it made **Phantom Films** a lot of money. Now, a decade later, the sequel has become a courtroom battle before it even has a release date. ![Phantom Studios — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/2/2c/Phantom_Films_logo.jpeg) ## The Lawsuit **Phantom Studios** has filed a ₹250 crore lawsuit in the **Bombay High Court** against **JioStar**, alleging that **Queen 2** is an unauthorised sequel that infringes on their intellectual property. The production house claims it owns 50 per cent of the IP rights to Queen — including sequel, prequel, and derivative rights — and that the makers of Queen 2 never sought its consent. > **"Bollywood has historically been casual about IP — remakes, "inspired by" credits, and spiritual sequels are a cottage industry."** According to a Mid-Day report, Phantom issued a public notice back in April asserting its co-ownership of the Queen IP. Multiple communications were reportedly sent to filmmaker Vikas Bahl and to JioStar before the legal filing. None of them, the production house claims, produced a response. > "There was even a public notice put out and multiple communications sent to Vikas and JioStar as well, informing them before this step was taken." — Source close to Phantom Studios The timing is pointed. Queen 2 recently wrapped principal photography. Kangana shared celebration photos from set on Instagram, looking triumphant. The film has entered post-production. For Phantom to file now — after filming is complete but before release — is a classic IP pressure move. The message is clear: *you built this without us, and we're not letting it go quietly.* ![Phantom Films — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/2/2c/Phantom_Films_logo.jpeg) ## The Phantom History To understand the lawsuit, you have to understand Phantom Films — the now-dissolved production collective founded by **Anurag Kashyap**, **Vikramaditya Motwane**, **Vikas Bahl**, and **Madhu Mantena** in 2011. Phantom was behind some of the best Hindi cinema of the decade: Gangs of Wasseypur, Lootera, Udta Punjab, and yes, Queen. The company dissolved in 2018 amid sexual harassment allegations against Vikas Bahl. The dissolution split the catalogue. And apparently, it split Queen's IP in a way that left Phantom Studios — the successor entity — holding half the rights. Anurag Kashyap himself has spoken about Queen's troubled origins. In a widely shared interview, he recalled that the studio partner "had no faith" in the film. Its executives literally went on vacation during its release week. Kashyap was the one who sat in the editing room, recognising what everyone else had missed. Now his legacy company is suing over the sequel. ![Gangs of Wasseypur — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/6/6a/Gangs_of_Wasseypur_poster.jpg)

## Kangana's Complicated Position Here's where it gets interesting. Kangana Ranaut is, let's be honest, not known for avoiding controversy. She's a sitting Member of Parliament. She's been through public feuds with practically every major figure in the industry. And Queen — the original — was the film that proved her right. It validated every claim she'd ever made about being an outsider who didn't need the industry's approval. Queen 2 was supposed to extend that legacy. Kangana reuniting with Vikas Bahl, returning to the character that changed everything. The fact that it now faces a ₹250 crore legal challenge before anyone's seen a frame is the kind of irony that writes itself. ## What Happens Next The Bombay High Court will hear the matter, and the outcome could set a significant precedent for how sequel rights are handled in Indian cinema. Bollywood has historically been casual about IP — remakes, "inspired by" credits, and spiritual sequels are a cottage industry. But a formal legal dispute over a franchise sequel, with a claim this large, forces the issue into the open. For diaspora audiences who remember Queen as one of those rare films that actually captured something true about a young Indian woman finding herself — in Paris, of all places — the legal drama is a reminder that behind every beloved film is a business. And business, as always, is personal. Neither Kangana Ranaut, Vikas Bahl, nor JioStar have issued official statements on the lawsuit at the time of writing.
